# India Braces for Its First Weak Monsoon in Three Years — and the Diaspora Should Be Watching

## A developing super El Niño threatens to slash rainfall to 92 per cent of normal, imperilling crops, inflating food prices, and testing a rural economy that NRI remittance dollars help sustain

The India Meteorological Department's long-range forecast, released in late April, delivered numbers that farmers, commodity traders, and diaspora families have been dreading: India's 2026 southwest monsoon is projected to deliver roughly 92 per cent of the Long Period Average — the first officially below-normal season since 2023 and only the second since the devastating 2018 drought.

The culprit is a textbook super El Niño, one that climate scientists are already comparing to the monsters of 1997 and 2015. Sea-surface temperatures in the central Pacific have surged past the 2°C anomaly threshold, and most dynamical models predict the event will persist through January 2027, making it the longest El Niño episode of the twenty-first century.

### Where the Pain Will Land First

The IMD's regional breakdown paints a stark picture. Punjab, Haryana, and western Rajasthan — India's grain belt — face the highest probability of deficient rainfall, with a 35 per cent chance that seasonal totals could dip below the critical 90-per-cent-of-LPA marker. For a region that produces nearly 40 per cent of India's wheat and a significant share of its rice, even a moderate shortfall can cascade through the supply chain within weeks.

At the other extreme, parts of Tamil Nadu and coastal Andhra Pradesh may see excessive rainfall during the northeast monsoon season later in the year — a pattern consistent with previous El Niño years that dumped record rain on Chennai in 2015 and again in 2023.

Delhi, already reeling from groundwater depletion, is expected to receive below-average monsoon rainfall, compounding what water-resource experts describe as an emerging urban water crisis. The capital's Yamuna reservoirs were at 60 per cent capacity entering May; a weak monsoon could push rationing into the autumn.

### The Inflation Equation

India's consumer price index is acutely sensitive to monsoon performance. Pulses, oilseeds, and coarse cereals — staples for hundreds of millions — are almost entirely rain-fed. The Reserve Bank of India's latest monetary policy report flagged El Niño as a "material upside risk to food inflation," noting that every one-percentage-point deviation in monsoon rainfall from normal historically adds 30 to 50 basis points to headline CPI.

Kharif sowing, which begins in June, is already under a cloud. Seed companies report that farmers in Maharashtra and Karnataka are delaying purchases, waiting for clearer rain signals before committing capital. A study published this month by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology found that El Niño years see over 10 per cent declines in kharif output across major producing states — a finding that has rattled the commodities desk at NCDEX.

### Why the Diaspora Cannot Afford to Look Away

For the roughly 18 million Indians living abroad, the monsoon is not an abstraction. NRI remittances — which crossed $125 billion in fiscal year 2025-26 according to the World Bank — flow disproportionately to rural households that depend on agriculture. A weak monsoon means those remittance dollars stretch further in one sense (the rupee has already breached 96 against the dollar, boosting purchasing power) but are needed more desperately in another.

Diaspora families with farmland in Punjab, Haryana, or Uttar Pradesh face a double bind: crop insurance penetration in India remains below 30 per cent, and the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana has been plagued by delayed payouts. Many NRI landowners rely on sharecroppers who are themselves one bad season away from distress.

The ripple effects extend beyond agriculture. Weak monsoons have historically correlated with slower GDP growth — the 2014-15 El Niño, for instance, shaved an estimated 0.5 percentage points off India's annual growth rate. For NRIs invested in Indian equities, mutual funds, or real estate, the monsoon forecast is a leading indicator that deserves attention.

### What Comes Next

The IMD will release its updated regional forecast in the first week of June, and the monsoon's actual onset over Kerala — typically around June 1 — will provide the first hard data. Climate scientists caution that super El Niño events can evolve rapidly; the 1997 event, for example, shifted from moderate to extreme within six weeks, upending forecasts.

For now, the government is taking no chances. The agriculture ministry has instructed states to pre-position drought-relief funds, and the National Disaster Management Authority has issued advisories to all El Niño-vulnerable districts. The central government is also reportedly considering releasing buffer stocks of rice and wheat early to stabilise prices if kharif planting falters.

The monsoon remains India's most consequential annual event — a four-month season that determines whether 600 million people eat well or go hungry. In 2026, with a super El Niño building and global food prices already elevated by conflict and supply-chain disruptions, the stakes have rarely been higher. For the diaspora, it is a reminder that the weather in Chandigarh and Chennai is never truly a world away.
